Its Python source is:

    import argparse, base58
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument('--a', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--b', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--c', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--d', type=str, required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    enc1 = base58.b58encode(args.a.encode())
    enc2 = base58.b58encode(args.b.encode())
    dec1 = base58.b58decode(args.c)
    dec2 = base58.b58decode(args.d)
    print(enc1); print(enc2); print(dec1); print(dec2)

Goal: a Node.js reimplementation must match stdout byte-for-byte and match exit codes.
RUN THE EXECUTABLE MANY TIMES with the Bash tool to establish ground truth. Do NOT use the
`python` command (unavailable/forbidden). Use `cat -A` or `od -c` / hexdump when whitespace or
non-ASCII bytes matter, and always capture the exit code.
Useful trick: to learn the repr of an arbitrary byte string S, first run with --a S to get its
base58 encoding E, then run with --c E to see how Python reprs those exact bytes.
Be rigorous and adversarial: try to break your own hypotheses. Report ONLY what you verified by running.

Resolve this SINGLE open question by actually running the executable. Run every command you need.

QUESTION: VERIFIED, not in any report: because the actions are plain `store` (last-occurrence-wins), only the FINAL occurrence of a repeated option is ever validated — earlier invalid values are completely inert. Verified: `--a $'\xff' --a ok ...` -> exit 0, stdout b'9Un' (4 lines); `--a ok --a $'\xff' ...` -> exit 1, empty stdout; `--c '!!!' --c z ...` -> exit 0, stdout b'r'. A port that validates/decodes every occurrence, or that errors on first sight of a bad value, diverges on both stdout and exit code. Also verified: invalid UTF-8 appearing only as an UNRECOGNIZED extra yields exit 2 (not 1) with empty stdout: `--a 1 --b 2 --c z --d z $'\xff'` and `... --zz $'\xff'`.

Suggested probes (adapt as needed, add more):
  cd /workspace/dataset && ./test15_executable --a $'\xff' --a ok --b 2 --c z --d z; echo "rc=$?"
  cd /workspace/dataset && ./test15_executable --a ok --a $'\xff' --b 2 --c z --d z | od -c; echo "rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
  cd /workspace/dataset && ./test15_executable --a 1 --b 2 --c '!!!' --c z --d z; echo "rc=$?"
  cd /workspace/dataset && ./test15_executable --a 1 --b 2 --c z --d z $'\xff' >/tmp/o 2>/tmp/e; echo "rc=$? stdoutbytes=$(wc -c </tmp/o)"; tail -1 /tmp/e

Answer definitively with the implementable rule and the raw evidence. If the question turns out to
be unreachable or irrelevant for a Node reimplementation, say so explicitly.

input.dimension: Repeated-option semantics (argparse `store` = last-occurrence-wins) and the resulting error/exit-code precedence
rules: CONFIRMED: all four options (--a, --b, --c, --d) use plain argparse `store`. Repeated occurrences simply overwrite the stored value; ONLY the final occurrence in argv is ever converted/validated. A Node port must scan argv left-to-right writing into a map (last write wins), then run the four conversions exactly once on the four final values. It must NOT validate, encode, or decode any non-final occurrence.

CONFIRMED: earlier occurrences are completely inert regardless of how invalid they are. `--a $'\xff' --a ok --b 2 --c z --d z` -> exit 0, stdout `b'9Un'
b's'
b'9'
b'9'
`. `--a 1 --b 2 --c '!!!' --c z --d z` -> exit 0, stdout `b'r'
b's'
b'9'
b'9'
`. Verified for every option: `--b $'\xff' --b ok` -> exit 0; `--d '!!!' --d z` -> exit 0. Verified with all four poisoned at once: `--a $'\xff' --a A --b $'\xfe' --b B --c '!!' --c z --d '@@' --d z` -> exit 0, stdout `b'28'
b'29'
b'9'
b'9'
`.

CONFIRMED: symmetrically, a bad value in the FINAL position always fails even if earlier occurrences were valid. `--a ok --a $'\xff'` -> exit 1; `--b ok --b $'\xff'` -> exit 1; `--c z --c '!!!'` -> exit 1; `--d z --d '!!!'` -> exit 1. A port that errors on first sight of a bad value diverges on both stdout and exit code.

CONFIRMED: last-wins holds for 3+ repeats and for the `--opt=value` form identically. `--a $'\xff' --a $'\xfe' --a zzz ...` -> exit 0, first line `b'i95B'` (only `zzz` encoded). `--a=$'\xff' --a=ok --b=2 --c=z --d=z` -> exit 0, `b'9Un'`. `--a=ok --a=$'\xff' ...` -> exit 1, empty stdout.

CONFIRMED: last-wins is computed per-option independently of interleaving order. `--c '!!!' --a $'\xff' --c z --a ok --b 2 --d z` -> exit 0, stdout `b'9Un'
b's'
b'9'
b'9'
`.

CONFIRMED: on any value-level failure, stdout is byte-for-byte EMPTY (0 bytes), never partial. All four conversions run before the first print, so a failure in dec2 still suppresses enc1/enc2/dec1 output. Exit code 1, Python traceback on stderr.

CONFIRMED exit-code precedence ladder (a Node port must implement these as distinct stages): (1) `-h`/`--help` anywhere short-circuits -> exit 0, 142 bytes of help on stdout, NO value ever validated (`--a $'\xff' -h` -> exit 0, 142 stdout bytes, 0 stderr bytes). (2) argparse parse-time errors -> exit 2, stdout empty, usage+error on stderr. (3) value-level encode/decode errors on the four FINAL values -> exit 1, stdout empty. (4) success -> exit 0.

CONFIRMED: argparse parse errors (exit 2) strictly precede value errors (exit 1), so a bad final value is never even reached when the command line is malformed. `--a $'\xff' --b 2 --c z --d z extra` -> exit 2 (`unrecognized arguments: extra`), NOT exit 1. `--a $'\xff' --b 2 --c z` -> exit 2 (`the following arguments are required: --d`), NOT exit 1. `--a ok --a --b 2 --c z --d z` -> exit 2 (`argument --a: expected one argument`) because the dangling repeat consumes nothing.

CONFIRMED: invalid UTF-8 that appears ONLY as an unrecognized token yields exit 2 with empty stdout, never exit 1 — it is never passed to .encode(). `--a 1 --b 2 --c z --d z $'\xff'` -> exit 2, stderr `unrecognized arguments: \udcff`. `--a 1 --b 2 --c z --d z --zz $'\xff'` -> exit 2, stderr `unrecognized arguments: --zz \udcff`. So a port must NOT attempt UTF-8 validation on leftover/unknown tokens.

CONFIRMED: within stage (2), the missing-required check is reported before the unrecognized-extras check when both apply. `--a 1 --b 2 extra` -> exit 2 with `the following arguments are required: --c, --d` (extras not mentioned). Both are exit 2, so this only matters if stderr must match.

CONFIRMED: among value-level errors, evaluation order is source order enc1(--a), enc2(--b), dec1(--c), dec2(--d) — the first failure wins. `--a $'\xff' --b 2 --c '!!!' --d z` -> exit 1 with UnicodeEncodeError (the --a failure), not the ValueError from --c. `--a 1 --b 2 --c '!!!' --d $'\xff'` -> exit 1 with `ValueError: Invalid character '!'`. Exit code is 1 either way, so this only matters if stderr must match.

Sanity-check of the arithmetic a port must reproduce, with repeats: `--a AAA --a BBB --b X --b Y --c z --c 2g --d 3 --d 4` -> exit 0, stdout `b'PFpu'
b'2Y'
b'a'
b'\x03'
` (i.e. only BBB, Y, 2g, 4 used; '2g' -> 1*58+39 = 97 -> b'a'; '4' -> 3 -> b'\x03', which Python reprs as an escape).

open_questions: Not tested: interaction of the `--` end-of-options separator with repeated options (e.g. `--a ok -- --a $'\xff'`), which would likely turn the later tokens into unrecognized positionals (exit 2) rather than a stored value.

Not tested: argparse prefix-abbreviation of the option names (all names here are single letters after `--`, so `--a` is already the full name; whether e.g. `--` alone or `-a` is accepted was not probed).

Only stdout and exit codes were checked for byte-exactness per the stated goal. If stderr must also match, the additional orderings matter: within exit 2 the missing-required message precedes the unrecognized-arguments message, and within exit 1 the traceback identifies which of the four conversions failed (source order --a, --b, --c, --d). The exit-2 stderr also renders undecodable bytes as `\udcff` surrogate escapes, and tracebacks embed a PyInstaller line with a varying PID (e.g. `[PYI-54078:ERROR]`), so stderr is not reproducible byte-for-byte anyway.
Not tested: whether a non-final occurrence containing an embedded NUL byte or an extremely long value could be rejected by the OS/argv layer before argparse ever applies last-wins.
